title: DNS Zone Transfer over TLS
summary: DNS zone transfers are sent in cleartext, so eavesdroppers can collect a zone's contents, and TSIG authorizes clients but does not add confidentiality. This document specifies using TLS for zone transfers, called XFR over TLS (XoT). It also updates RFC 1995, RFC 5936 and RFC 7766 on efficient use of TCP connections.

plainLanguage.summary: When one name server copies its list of names to another, anyone nearby could read it. This document wraps the copying in a secret tunnel.

questions: which port does zone transfer over tls use
subtitle: Encrypting DNS zone transfers (AXFR and IXFR) with TLS 1.3 so eavesdroppers cannot collect a zone's contents.

tldr.problem: DNS zone transfers normally travel in cleartext, so anyone watching the network can collect the full contents of a zone. TSIG authorizes clients but does not encrypt anything.
tldr.mechanism: XFR over TLS (XoT) runs AXFR and IXFR inside TLS 1.3, normally on port 853, with ALPN token dot, strict server authentication and client authorization by mutual TLS or by an IP ACL plus TSIG/SIG(0). The document also tightens TCP connection reuse for all zone transfers.
tldr.outcome: Zone contents are protected from passive surveillance, but only if the whole transfer group uses XoT. It does not hide that a zone exists, who hosts it, or (fully) zone activity.

today: RFC 9103 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 1995, RFC 5936 and RFC 7766.

sections.title: Why Zone Transfers Need Encryption
sections.content:
Much DNS privacy work has focused on stub-to-recursive queries (DNS over TLS, DNS over HTTPS). Zone transfers got little attention. RFC 5936 specifies TSIG for authorizing zone transfer clients and for data integrity, but expresses no need for confidentiality, and TSIG offers no encryption.

The RFC argues that exposing a full zone is a privacy risk: names can contain personal information or hint at locations and other organizations, and the full set of IP addresses helps reconnaissance and attack targeting. Because AXFR and IXFR typically run over TCP, wrapping them in TLS based closely on DoT is a simple step. This document specifies using TLS 1.3 or later for that.
sections.plainLanguage: A zone is like a school's full class list. Sending the whole list on an open postcard lets anyone read it, so XoT puts it in a sealed envelope.

sections.title: Threat Model and Scope
sections.content:
The threat model treats the current contents and size of the zone as sensitive. It does not treat as sensitive the existence of a zone, the act of transferring it, or the identities of the name servers (including hidden primaries). It also does not consider attacks on the mechanisms that trigger a transfer, such as NOTIFY messages.

The RFC notes that using XoT signals that the zone owner wants confidentiality, so it could be blocked, for example by blocking port 853. It also says that preventing eavesdropping is orthogonal to preventing zone enumeration (for example NSEC walking), though both protect the same information.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is to hide what is written in the list, not the fact that two servers are talking.

sections.title: How Existing Transfers Work
sections.content:
A primary holds the master copy and a secondary fetches it. The original design polled with SOA queries; RFC 1996 NOTIFY and RFC 1995 IXFR (incremental transfer) added prompt propagation. RFC 5936 redefined AXFR (full transfer) and requires TCP.

A typical exchange is a NOTIFY over UDP, an SOA request to learn the primary's serial number, and then an AXFR or IXFR request if the primary's serial is higher. IXFR may start over UDP and retry over TCP, or fall back to AXFR. The RFC notes that BIND and NSD do IXFR over TCP by default in their latest releases, but often close the connection after one IXFR.

The RFC also considers whether NOTIFY and SOA exchanges leak information. Unencrypted NOTIFY messages identify the configured secondaries on the primary, and an SOA response from a hidden server only leaks the SOA serial lag of its downstream secondaries.
sections.plainLanguage: One server tells another 'my list changed', the other checks the version number, and then it asks for either the whole list or just the changes.

sections.title: Better TCP Connection Use
sections.content:
This document updates RFC 1995, RFC 5936 and RFC 7766. Implementations of XFR over TCP MUST use RFC 7766 to optimize TCP connections. Clients SHOULD reuse an open connection to the same primary for new XFR requests and SOA queries. Valid reasons not to include a configured request limit, an exhausted message ID pool, many timeouts, or an edns-tcp-keepalive timeout of 0 from the server.

Servers MUST handle multiple concurrent IXFR requests, and multiple concurrent AXFR sessions, on one connection. AXFR response streams MAY be intermingled, and clients that pipeline AXFR requests MUST handle that. Clients sending several XFRs MAY choose not to pipeline them. Implementations SHOULD use the edns-tcp-keepalive option to manage persistent connections and SHOULD use one connection for both AXFR and IXFR to the same primary.

A server MAY limit concurrent transfers and SHOULD return SERVFAIL when the limit is hit. RFC 7766 is updated so that for each protocol used on top of TCP there SHOULD be no more than one connection for regular queries and one for zone transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of hanging up and redialing for every request, keep one phone line open and ask several things on it.

sections.title: How XoT Works
sections.content:
The secondary opens the TLS connection, so it is the TLS client and the primary is the TLS server. The ALPN token dot MUST be selected in the handshake, implementations MUST use only TLS 1.3 or later, and the connection SHOULD use port 853 unless both sides agree on another port.

For a transfer to count as protected, all XFR requests and responses for the zone MUST go over TLS. The client MUST authenticate the server using an authentication domain name with a Strict Privacy profile (RFC 8310). The server MUST validate that the client is authorized, using mutual TLS, or an IP-based ACL combined with a valid TSIG/SIG(0) signature on the request. If only one method is used, mTLS is preferred.

If a XoT server receives non-XoT traffic it will not answer on a TLS connection, it SHOULD respond with REFUSED and extended DNS error code 21, Not Supported. Clients should then avoid sending that query type for a reasonable period, for example one hour. This does not define authoritative DoT.
sections.plainLanguage: The copying server knocks on a special door, shows it is really the right server, and the other side checks it is allowed in before handing over the list.

sections.title: Authentication Choices
sections.content:
The RFC compares mechanisms by data origin authentication, channel confidentiality and channel authentication. TSIG and SIG(0) give data origin authentication. Opportunistic TLS can fall back to unauthenticated TLS or cleartext, so it is not considered useful for XoT. Strict TLS gives confidentiality and authenticates the server. Mutual TLS authenticates both ends. An IP ACL on the primary authenticates the client, but it can only be enforced once a request arrives on an established connection unless a per-connection ACL is used.

The conclusion is that mutual TLS alone is a standalone solution, while secondary-side Strict TLS plus a primary-side IP ACL with TSIG/SIG(0) is acceptable. An ACL alone could be attacked by spoofing, and TSIG alone could be exposed if messages were accidentally sent in cleartext. ZONEMD is described as complementary and orthogonal.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several ways to prove who you are, like a password, a name badge or a guest list. The best setup has both sides check each other's badge.

sections.title: Padding, Policy and Migration
sections.content:
AXoT and IXoT responses may be padded to hide zone size and update activity. Secondaries MUST be resilient to padded responses, including 'empty' AXoT responses carrying only an OPT record with the padding option. The last AXoT message MUST still contain the same SOA as the first. Specific padding policies are out of scope. Name compression limits individual responses to roughly 16 KB, so implementations may offer a way to disable it.

Protection needs consistent policy: the whole transfer group MUST use XoT for both AXFRs and IXFRs, otherwise a weak link remains. A policy MUST say whether mutual TLS and/or an IP ACL with TSIG/SIG(0) is used. For migration, servers may allow a client to use either XoT or TCP, but such options MUST only be used in a 'migration mode'. A TLS proxy in front of the primary is a simple way to enable server-side XoT.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the group has to use the sealed envelope, or the whole trick fails. Extra filler can hide how big the list really is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: XoT protects against an attacker collecting entire zones by eavesdropping on cleartext transfers. It does not mitigate inferring zone activity from transfer sizes and timing (even with padding), identifying hidden primaries by watching encrypted connections, or obtaining zone contents through zone enumeration. DoT security concerns are in RFC 7858 and RFC 8310. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope hides the words, but a watcher can still see that mail is going back and forth and roughly how thick it is.
